t: Maximum Capacity Within Budget — Sort, Prefix-Max Capacity and Binary Search
o: You may pick one or two distinct machines whose total cost is strictly less than `budget`, maximizing total capacity. Example 1: costs 4 and 3 sum to 7 < 8, capacities 1+7=8. Example 2 shows a single machine (cost 4 < 7, capacity 6) is allowed. Example 3 shows duplicates are fine (2+2=4 < 5, capacity 9). With n up to 1e5, the O(n²) pairwise scan is too slow, so we need sorting plus a fast lookup of the best capacity among cheaper machines.
k: Strict inequality means for a fixed machine of cost c we need partners with cost < budget - c.
Sorting by cost lets a prefix-maximum of capacity answer 'best capacity among all machines cheaper than X' in O(log n).
Remember to also consider picking just one machine.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute Force Over All Choices
a.i: Try every single machine and every pair, checking the strict budget constraint directly. Simple and obviously correct; only viable for small n.
s: Loop over each machine i; if costs[i] < budget record capacity[i].
Loop over pairs i<j; if costs[i]+costs[j] < budget record the capacity sum.

a.n: Approach 2: Sort by Cost + Prefix Maximum Capacity + Binary Search
a.i: Sort machines by cost. For each machine i (as the more expensive of a pair), every machine j < i in sorted order is cheaper; the best partner capacity for the constraint cost[j] < budget - costs[i] is a prefix maximum, found by binary searching the cut point.
s: Create (cost, capacity) pairs sorted by cost; build arrays cs (sorted costs) and pre (prefix max of capacity).
For each i, if cs[i] < budget update the answer with the single machine.
Binary search the largest index j < i with cs[j] < budget - cs[i]; update with capacity[i] + pre[j].
a.t: O(n log n) — sorting dominates; each element does one binary search
a.sp: O(n) — sorted copy and prefix-max array

w: Use the sorted + prefix-max approach in interviews; mention the brute force only as a baseline. Pitfalls: forgetting the single-machine option, using <= instead of < for the budget, and off-by-one errors at the binary-search boundary (we need cost strictly less than budget - c). Follow-ups: generalize to at most m machines (meet-in-the-middle or knapsack-style DP).
